evidence.claim: Old Highway 10 links rural towns beside North Dakota’s interstate
evidence.quote: An alternative to Interstate 94 between Mandan and Dickinson, this route offers a leisurely drive through lovely, rural countryside

evidence.claim: Old Red Old Ten follows old Highway 10 between Dickinson and Mandan, parallel to Interstate 94.
evidence.quote: Begins at the Mandan Depot on Main Street in Mandan and leads west along Old Highway 10 to Dickinson.

evidence.claim: North Dakota Tourism presents the scenic byway as a leisurely drive through rural countryside, with small-town museums and landmarks along the way.
evidence.quote: An alternative to Interstate 94 between Mandan and Dickinson, this route offers a leisurely drive through lovely, rural countryside

evidence.claim: Its August 2021 guide describes blacktop with gravel sections between New Salem and Glen Ullin and on the Curlew Loop toward Almont.
evidence.quote: Although Old Ten is a "blacktop," watch the map for the gravel section(s) of the route; between New Salem and Glen Ullin or on the Curlew Loop spur, en route to/from Almont.

evidence.claim: The name reaches back to the Red Trail, one of the routes identified by color before numbered highways. Highway 10 followed that trail era.
evidence.quote: Before highways, there were trails across the country designated by color names. The Old Red Trail originally extended from Seattle to New York City. Eventually it became old Highway 10 from Seattle to Ludington, Mich.

evidence.claim: Rail transport also shaped the towns beside the road. Sims began as a coal town on the Northern Pacific Railway in 1883. When the railway straightened its main line in 1947, it cut off Sims and Almont, having less need for frequent servicing stops.
evidence.quote: The town's fortunes remained closely tied to the railway's, and when NP in 1947 straightened out their mainline (now that trains no longer needed as frequent servicing stops), Sims along with Almont was cut off from railroad access.

evidence.claim: Drive east from Dickinson toward Richardton and Assumption Abbey, then through Hebron and Glen Ullin.
evidence.quote: Mandan, Almont, New Salem, Glen Ullin, Hebron, Richardton

evidence.claim: The Sims church and Salem Sue at New Salem are later landmarks on this eastbound journey, which ends at Mandan's depot on Main Street.
evidence.quote: Points of Interest Mandan Depot Salem Sue at New Salem Sims Church Fort Sauerkraut at Hebron Dacotah Clayworks at Hebron Assumption Abbey at Richardton

evidence.claim: That depot dates to 1930, a replacement built at the railroad site.
evidence.quote: The existing "beanery" lunchroom and depot were constructed in 1928 and 1930, respectively as replacements at the site.

evidence.claim: parallel to Interstate 94
evidence.quote: runs parallel to Interstate 94.

evidence.claim: with small-town museums and landmarks along the way
evidence.quote: Travelers can slow down to enjoy small town amenities, local museums, events, lodging, eateries, arts and craft shops and auto services.

evidence.claim: Sims began as a coal town on the Northern Pacific Railway in 1883.
evidence.quote: Sims was founded in 1883 as a coal town along the Northern Pacific Railway

evidence.claim: ends at Mandan's depot on Main Street
evidence.quote: Begins at the Mandan Depot on Main Street in Mandan and leads west along Old Highway 10 to Dickinson.

evidence.claim: The Benedictine community at Richardton has changed both address and name. Founded in 1893 by a monk from Einsiedeln Abbey in Switzerland, it was first called St. Gall's.
evidence.quote: Assumption Abbey, located in Richardton, North Dakota, is a Benedictine abbey of the American-Cassinese Congregation (different from the Subiaco Cassinese Congregation), founded in 1893 by a monk from the Einsiedeln Abbey in Switzerland.

evidence.claim: The monks moved from the north shore of Devils Lake to Richardton in June 1899 and renamed their community St. Mary's Priory.
evidence.quote: Originally called St. Gall’s, the monks relocated from the north shore of Devils Lake to the city of Richardton on June 24, 1899, and changed the name to St. Mary’s Priory.

evidence.claim: In 1903, the Holy See raised it to an abbey, and founder Vincent de Paul Wehrle became its first abbot.
evidence.quote: In 1903 the Holy See raised the community to the rank of abbey and Vincent de Paul Wehrle, the founder, was elected first abbot.

evidence.claim: it was first called St. Gall's
evidence.quote: Originally called St. Gall’s

evidence.claim: The Assumption Abbey name followed in 1928, when the community and its property were incorporated under that title.
evidence.quote: On October 29, 1928, the community and its property was incorporated under the title Assumption Abbey.

evidence.claim: The railroad needed coal and water when Sims was founded in 1883. Coal mining and a brickyard helped the settlement grow, but in 1947 the Northern Pacific straightened its main line and left Sims without rail access.
evidence.quote: Sims was founded in 1883 as a coal town along the Northern Pacific Railway, who had reached Bismarck ten years earlier and now needed to take a detour to access coal and water. Coal mining and the town's brickyard helped Sims grow

evidence.claim: The church remains active even though its congregation lives elsewhere.
evidence.quote: The congregation still has roughly 50 members, even though they do not live in Sims.

evidence.claim: Its buildings mark two stages of that religious community: the 1884 building combined church and residence and survives as the parsonage; the later church was begun in 1896 and completed in 1900. The restored parsonage houses the Sims Historical Society Museum.
evidence.quote: Sims Scandinavian Lutheran Church was built in 1896 and completed in 1900. An earlier 1884 combination church and residence remains today as the parsonage to the church.

evidence.claim: in 1947 the Northern Pacific straightened its main line and left Sims without rail access
evidence.quote: when NP in 1947 straightened out their mainline (now that trains no longer needed as frequent servicing stops), Sims along with Almont was cut off from railroad access.

evidence.claim: The restored parsonage houses the Sims Historical Society Museum.
evidence.quote: The church parsonage has also been restored and is home to the Sims Historical Society Museum.

evidence.claim: The 2021 North Dakota Tourism guide identifies gravel between New Salem and Glen Ullin and on the Curlew Loop toward Almont.
evidence.quote: watch the map for the gravel section(s) of the route; between New Salem and Glen Ullin or on the Curlew Loop spur, en route to/from Almont.

evidence.claim: Salem Sue arrived in three pieces. The hollow fiberglass Holstein was made in La Crosse, Wisconsin, then transported and assembled in New Salem.
evidence.quote: The cow, which is hollow, was constructed by Sculpture Mfg. Co in La Crosse, Wisconsin and then transported in 3 parts before being put together.

evidence.claim: Local farmers and residents donated toward the $40,000 sculpture, built in 1974 and sponsored by the New Salem Lions Club to honor the dairy industry.
evidence.quote: Salem Sue was built in 1974 for $40,000, by donations from local farmers and residents, and was sponsored by the New Salem Lions Club in honor of the local dairy farming industry.

evidence.claim: At 38 feet high and 50 feet long, she stands on School Hill near Interstate 94 and is visible for several miles.
evidence.quote: The statue stands 38 feet (12 m) high and 50 feet (15 m) long

evidence.claim: Even the maintenance fund suits its subject: a milk-can-shaped donation bin at the bottom of the hill helps pay for upkeep and repainting.
evidence.quote: an at-will donation bin, shaped like a milk can, sits at the bottom of the hill to help maintain the property and re-paint the cow as needed.

evidence.claim: The 38-foot fiberglass Holstein stands on School Hill and can be seen for several miles.
evidence.quote: It sits on School Hill near Interstate 94 off exit 127 S and can be viewed for several miles.

evidence.claim: she stands on School Hill near Interstate 94 and is visible for several miles
evidence.quote: It sits on School Hill near Interstate 94 off exit 127 S and can be viewed for several miles.

evidence.claim: Between Hebron and Richardton, the route passes the 2,000-acre Schnell Recreation Area, a nature preserve.
evidence.quote: the Schnell Recreation Area, a 2,000-acre nature preserve located between Hebron and Richardton.

evidence.claim: Wehrle later became the first bishop of the Diocese of Bismarck, in 1910.
evidence.quote: Wehrle would go on to become the first bishop of the Diocese of Bismarck in 1910.

evidence.claim: The post office also closed in 1947, with mail redirected through Almont.
evidence.quote: The post office was founded in 1883 and closed in 1947, with mail routed through Almont, to the south.
